PSX Tracker guide

Realistic returns on the Pakistan Stock Exchange

People ask how much they can make on PSX. There is no honest fixed number. Outcomes depend on what you buy, how long you hold, what you pay in costs and taxes, and how markets behave. This page frames the building blocks without selling a dream.

By PSX Tracker · Updated 23 September 2026

Two engines: income and price change

Dividends (and similar distributions) are cash or value you may receive while you hold. Capital gains appear when you sell above your cost; capital losses appear when you sell below.

A stock can pay dividends and still lose money overall if the price falls more than the income you received. Looking at only one number hides that story.

Why someone else’s return is not yours

Index charts and influencer screenshots leave out your entry price, fees, taxes and behaviour. They also leave out periods of painful drawdown.

Your measurable return is what your own ledger says after costs.

Costs and taxes are part of return

Commission, other trading charges, and tax on gains or dividend withholding reduce what you keep. Rules change; verify with current FBR and broker information.

If you ignore costs, every strategy looks better on paper than in your bank account.

Risk is not optional

Equity prices can fall for long stretches. Company-specific news can gap a stock overnight. Concentration in one tip amplifies that risk.

Money needed soon for tuition, medical costs or debt payments is usually a poor match for volatile shares.

How to review your own results

Separate unrealized marks on open positions from realized results on closed trades, and track dividend income on its own line.

PSX Tracker surfaces those lenses so you can judge your process with facts — not vibes.

This guide is educational only. It is not investment, tax, legal or religious advice. Rules, fees and tax rates change — confirm details with your broker, SECP/PSX sources, FBR guidance and qualified advisors before you act.

Where a return can come from

You are paid, if you are paid, in two ways. The company sends a dividend, or the price you can sell at is different from the price you paid. Both can be negative in the sense that matters: the dividend can be cut, and the price can be lower. Fees and taxes sit on top and make the amount you keep smaller than the headline move.

The index is a basket with rules, weighted toward large companies, rebalanced on a published method. Your portfolio is whatever you bought. It can beat the index by luck or skill, and it can lag the index while the index itself is down. Comparing them is useful. Confusing them is how people say “the market did well” in a year their own book did not.

A fund’s return is the change in NAV plus distributions, after the fees the document describes. It is not the KSE-100’s return, even for an equity fund, because the holdings and the fees differ.

Past numbers are a record, not a forecast

A decade in which an index rose a lot does not owe you the same decade again. Inflation, the currency, political news, and a handful of large stocks can dominate a period. Remove one or two names and the story of “the market” often changes. That is a reason to read the constituents, not a reason to memorize a percentage from a thumbnail.

Company history is the same shape. A fertilizer producer’s golden years are not a bond. A bank’s low provisions in a calm year are not a promise about the next credit cycle. The research guides on banks and cement are checklists of what to read, not predictions.

Your own past return, once the ledger is reconciled, is the only personal number. It includes your costs, your timing, and your mistakes. It is allowed to be worse than the index. That fact is information. It is not an insult and it is not a reason to double the next trade.

Costs and taxes are part of the result

Commission, taxes on commission, and CDC charges come off whether the trade worked or not. A strategy that trades every day pays them every day. A strategy that buys and holds pays them less often and still pays a spread and a tax when it eventually sells.

Dividend withholding means the cash you receive is less than the dividend the company declared. Record both, or your yield will look higher than the money that arrived. Capital gains tax, when it applies, comes off realized gains. Unrealized gains have not met that tax yet. The CGT guide explains the record you need without inventing the rate.

Fund management fees are easy to ignore because they are taken inside the NAV. They are still your cost. The factsheet states them. Subtracting them again on top of the NAV change would count them twice, so read whether the NAV you see is already net.

Risk is the chance you needed the money

A return that arrived after a 40 percent decline was not “about 15 percent a year” to the person who sold at the bottom to pay a bill. The path matters. If you cannot leave the money alone, you do not have the return the brochure averaged. You have the return up to the day you were forced out.

Concentration makes the path rougher. One stock, one sector, or one fund category is a bet that that story stays healthy. Diversification across names you understand reduces the chance that one story ends you. Diversification across names you do not understand reduces nothing you can act on.

Leverage and borrowed confidence from a group chat shorten the path further. A realistic plan states the amount, the horizon, and the reason you would sell. “It was going up” is not a reason you can reuse.

How to use the tracker in this light

Let the app show your return, the index, and the cash flows separately. A positive day on the index and a negative day on your book can both be true. The chart of daily moves is there so you can see the path. The total-return figure is there so you can see the destination so far, including dividends and costs you recorded.

If the figure surprises you, reconcile before you change your life. A missing dividend understates you. A duplicated buy overstates cost and understates the return. The surprise might be the data.

No screen on this site, and no paragraph in this guide, is a forecast or a suitable-for-you recommendation. The realistic expectation is modest, uneven, and entirely dependent on what you bought and what you paid away.

Common questions

How do PSX investors get a return?

From dividends and from a change in price. Both can be negative. Costs and taxes reduce what you keep.

Is a past index return a forecast?

No. A historical index move is context, not a promise for the next year.

Should I plan on a fixed yearly percentage?

No. Returns vary. A tracker shows what your own book did, which can differ from the index.
